title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without securing licenses from the rights holders before deployment. Udio launched a public AI music generation product, attracted millions of users, and only began formalizing licensing arrangements after lawsuits were filed. The problem was not a model malfunction but a procurement and legal compliance gap at the stage before training began, when the decision was made about which data to use.

The incident produced a cluster of distinct legal proceedings. Universal Music Group settled and moved to a licensing partnership. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging that over 30,000 recordings were used to train Udio's models, and when a judge declined to add those recordings to its original case, Sony filed a new lawsuit asserting them separately. Independent artists filed a class action that a court declined to dismiss. A musicians' union sued over the UMG settlement itself, and UMG asked for that case to be dismissed.

None of the lawsuits other than those that settled have reached a verdict, and the allegations of copying specific recordings remain claims rather than findings. What is established is that major rights holders and independent artists alike identified the same underlying question: whether using copyrighted sound recordings as training data, without authorization, constitutes infringement. The settlements show that licensing is now being treated as necessary going forward, but they do not resolve whether the original training was lawful.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which the record label accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The two companies have reached licensing agreements, and Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music. Users will be able to customize, stream, and share songs created through the platform, with artists compensated for their participation. UMG's CEO emphasized the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technology and business models.

Udio, a New York-based company founded by former Google DeepMind employees, was sued by UMG and other major record labels last year for allegedly copying hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to generate similar songs without permission or payment. The company had maintained that its AI learns from musical examples much like students study music. This settlement marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a major music label. The financial terms were not disclosed, though Udio has attracted millions of users since launching in 2024.
